name: Vārkarī sampradāya
regions: Maharashtra (Paṇḍharpūr on the Bhīmā/Candrabhāgā; Āḷandī; Dehu; Paiṭhaṇ; Sāsvaḍ; Tryambakeśvar; Maṅgaḷveḍhe; Terḍhokī)

tradition.text: Viṭṭhala has stood on the brick for twenty-eight yugas since Puṇḍalīka's time; the saints appear as a succession within it

scholarly.text: Paṇḍharpūr cult attested from the 12th–13th c.; the saint-tradition from Jñāneśvar and Nāmdev (late 13th c.); pālkhī processions organised from the late 17th c.

transmissions_received.what: initiation of Nivṛttināth by Gahinīnāth and through him of Jñāneśvar; the yoga of kuṇḍalinī described in Jñāneśvarī 6
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation: lineage verses at the close of Jñāneśvarī 18; tradition-account

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as scripture (Eknāthī Bhāgavat) and the Viṭṭhala māhātmyas
Eknāth's guru Janārdana Svāmī was a devotee of Dattātreya
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account (Eknāth's own verses on Janārdana; Mahīpati)

transmissions_given.what: Nāmdev's Hindi songs and example, revered by Kabīr and later northern Sants (Nāmdev's songs also stand in the Sikh scripture, context only)
a shared Marathi devotional idiom (Rāmdās's contemporaries and audience overlap)

distinctive_positions: God is worshipped as Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā, Pāṇḍuraṅga) of Paṇḍharpūr, standing on a brick with hands on hips — a form of Kṛṣṇa, identified also with Viṣṇu and, by some saints, with Śiva.
The name ('Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari', 'Viṭṭhala') and congregational singing (bhajan, kīrtan) are the main means; no renunciation is required — the householder's ordinary work becomes worship.

The twice-yearly vārī — walking pilgrimage to Paṇḍharpūr for the Āṣāḍhī and Kārtikī ekādaśīs, in diṇḍīs following the pālkhīs of Jñāneśvar and Tukārām — is the defining observance; initiation is by wearing the tuḷsī-bead necklace (māḷ).
Knowledge and devotion are held together: Jñāneśvar's non-dual teaching is crowned by devotion that continues after realization.
Saints of every caste and gender — tailor, potter, gardener, barber, Mahār, maidservant, courtesan's daughter, Kuṇbī, brahmin woman — are equally revered; the saints' company is itself the tīrtha.
Scripture is in Marathi; the 'three foundations' (prasthānatrayī) of the Vārkarīs are the Jñāneśvarī, the Eknāthī Bhāgavat and the Tukārām Gāthā.
The sequence of saints is pictured as one temple: Jñāneśvar the foundation, Nāmdev the walls, Eknāth the pillar, Tukārām the pinnacle (Bahiṇābāī).
summary: The Vārkarī tradition of Maharashtra worships Viṭṭhala of Paṇḍharpūr through the name, bhajan, kīrtan and the walking pilgrimage (vārī). It looks to a chain of Marathi saints from Jñāneśvar and Nāmdev (13th–14th c.) through Eknāth (16th c.) to Tukārām (17th c.), of every caste, whose songs and commentaries are its scripture. It joins non-dual knowledge (Jñāneśvar's Nāth-derived teaching) to devotion lived in the household.

name: Rāmānandī sampradāya

tradition.text: Rāmānanda lived 1299–1410 (Rāmānandī reckoning); the lineage descends from Rāma through Sītā, Hanumān and a succession of ṛṣis (independent account) or from Rāmānuja through Rāghavānanda (older account)

scholarly.text: Rāmānanda probably 14th–15th c. and poorly documented; the order's institutions (Galtā, the akhāṛās) consolidated 16th–18th c.

transmissions_received.what: descent through Rāghavānanda and qualified non-dualist doctrine
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account in older Rāmānandī guruparamparās; rejected by the 20th-c. independent faction (see dsp:ramanandi-descent-from-ramanuja)

transmissions_received.what: the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa's non-dual Rāma theology and Śabarī's nine devotions

transmissions_given.what: Kabīr, Raidās, Pīpā, Sena and Dhanna are counted Rāmānanda's disciples in the Bhaktamāl (tradition-account; disputed)
the Vaiṣṇava ascetic akhāṛās, largely Rāmānandī

distinctive_positions: Rāma with Sītā is the supreme Brahman; Hanumān is the model devotee-servant.
The six-syllable Rāma mantra (rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ) and the name 'Rāma' — the tāraka ('ferrying') mantra Śiva whispers to the dying at Kāśī — are the heart of practice.

Refuge in Rāma is open to all castes and to women; the tradition remembers Rāmānanda as initiating a weaver, a cobbler, a barber, a Jāṭ farmer, a Rajput king and women; the saying 'jāti pāṃti pūchai nahiṃ koī, hari ko bhajai so hari ko hoī' is ascribed to him in oral tradition.
Teaching in the vernacular: Tulsīdās's Awadhi Rāmcaritmānas became the scripture of north Indian Rāma-bhakti.
Rāma is both formless and with form; the name is greater than either (Tulsī).
Two styles of devotion: the ascetic (tyāgī, tapasvī) and the rasik, who contemplates the eternal love-play of Sītā and Rāma as a companion (sakhī).
Whether the order descends from Rāmānuja or is independent is debated within the tradition.
summary: The Rāmānandī sampradāya, the largest Vaiṣṇava ascetic order of north India, looks to Rāmānanda of Vārāṇasī and worships Rāma with Sītā through the Rāma mantra and name. Its hagiography (Nābhādās's Bhaktamāl) assigns Rāmānanda disciples of every caste, including Kabīr and Raidās; its greatest poet, Tulsīdās, made the Awadhi Rāmcaritmānas the devotional scripture of the Hindi-speaking world. It comprises ascetic (tyāgī) akhāṛās, householders, and a rasik branch.

name: Rasik Rāma-bhakti (Rasik sampradāya of the Rāmānandīs)

scholarly.text: from the late 16th c. (Agradās); flourishing in Ayodhyā from the 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: Contemplates the eternal, private love-play of Sītā and Rāma in the inner Ayodhyā (Sāketa) rather than the heroic epic deeds.
The practitioner takes an inner identity as a female companion (sakhī) of Sītā, serving the divine couple.
Sītā's grace is the gate to Rāma.
summary: A branch of the Rāmānandīs, traced to Agradās of Raivāsā, that practises the sweet (mādhurya) contemplation of Sītā and Rāma's eternal love in the manner of the Kṛṣṇa rasik traditions, the devotee taking the role of a sakhī.

name: Rādhāvallabha sampradāya

tradition.text: founded when Hita Harivaṃśa settled in Vṛndāvana and installed Rādhāvallabha (1535 CE)

transmissions_received.what: the Kṛṣṇa of Braj and the gopīs' love
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; the tradition itself traces its mantra to Rādhā, not to a human lineage

distinctive_positions: Rādhā is supreme: Kṛṣṇa is 'Rādhā's beloved' (Rādhāvallabha) and her devotee; the Rādhāvallabha temple has no image of Rādhā, her presence being marked by a seat (gaddī) beside Kṛṣṇa.
Hita — love — is the ultimate principle; the divine pair are its two forms.
The eternal love-play (nitya-vihāra) in the groves has no separation, no birth-story and no departure to Mathurā or Dvārakā; separation is felt only within union.
The devotee serves as a sakhī (companion), finding joy in the pair's joy (tatsukha), never seeking union for herself.
Rules of injunction and prohibition (vidhi-niṣedha) are secondary to love; liberation is not sought.
Hita Harivaṃśa received his mantra from Rādhā herself, so the sampradāya counts itself outside the four classical Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas.
summary: The Rādhāvallabha tradition of Vṛndāvana, founded by Hita Harivaṃśa in the 16th c., worships Rādhā as supreme and Kṛṣṇa as her beloved, contemplating their eternal, unbroken love-play in the groves. Its scripture is Harivaṃśa's Braj Hita Caurāsī (and, by its account, the Sanskrit Rādhā-sudhānidhi); love (hita) is its first principle and sakhī-like service its practice.

name: Haridāsī sampradāya (Sakhī sampradāya)
regions: Vṛndāvana (Nidhivan; Bāṅke Bihārī temple; Ṭaṭṭī Sthān)

tradition.text: Bāṅke Bihārī manifested at Nidhivan in response to Svāmī Haridās's singing (16th c.)

transmissions_given.what: Svāmī Haridās as the revered teacher of dhrupad singers (Tānsen) in north Indian music tradition

distinctive_positions: Worship in the grove (nikuñja-upāsanā): the natural, eternal pair (sahaja jorī) Kuñjabihārī and Śyāmā play for ever in the inner grove, beyond birth, avatāra and separation.
The devotee witnesses and serves as a sakhī; Svāmī Haridās is held to be the sakhī Lalitā.
Singing (dhrupad, samāj-gāyan) is itself worship.
Two branches: householder gosvāmīs serving Bāṅke Bihārī, and strict renunciants (virakta) of the Ṭaṭṭī Sthān.
Its relation to the Nimbārka sampradāya is disputed (see dsp:haridasi-nimbarka-affiliation).
summary: The Haridāsī or Sakhī sampradāya of Vṛndāvana, founded by the singer-saint Svāmī Haridās (16th c.), whose songs brought forth the image of Bāṅke Bihārī. It contemplates the ever-united divine pair in the inner grove as their sakhī and treats music as worship.

name: Mīrābāī's devotion (the Mīrā song-tradition)

transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account in songs attributed to her; chronologically doubted

transmissions_received.what: a meeting with Jīva Gosvāmī in Vṛndāvana

distinctive_positions: Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl / Giridhar Nāgar is her only husband; she refuses the conduct expected of a royal widow and the family's honour (lok-lāj, kul-kī-maryādā).
Love-in-separation (viraha) and madness of love (prem-dīvānī) are the texture of devotion.
The company of sādhus regardless of caste; the name as the jewel-treasure.
No formal sampradāya: the tradition lives in song, in shrines (Meṛtā, Chittor, Vṛndāvana) and in the hagiographies; several traditions claim her.
notes: Created by U26 because the coverage map lists Mīrābāī among 'other lineages' (A9); it is not a formal sampradāya. See REPORT.md.
summary: The devotion of Mīrābāī, a 16th-c. Rajput princess of Meṛtā married into Mewar, who took Kṛṣṇa as her husband and defied her in-laws. Her songs (mostly attributed) of love, separation and defiance are sung everywhere; the Bhaktamāl praises her for casting off family honour to worship Giridhar.

name: Mahānubhāva panth
regions: maṭhs in Punjab and the north-west (reported; verify)

tradition.text: Parameśvara has incarnated in every age; the five Kṛṣṇas culminate in Cakradhar

scholarly.text: founded by Cakradhar in the 1260s; Cakradhar left Maharashtra c. 1274

transmissions_received.what: Dattātreya counted among the five incarnations of Parameśvara
Kṛṣṇa of the Gītā and Bhāgavata as an incarnation of Parameśvara
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; the classic poems retell Bhāgavata episodes

distinctive_positions: Four eternal, distinct realities: souls (jīva), deities (devatā), the world (prapañca) and the one Supreme (Parameśvara).
Parameśvara alone gives liberation; he has incarnated as the five Kṛṣṇas (pañca-kṛṣṇa): Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu (Guṇḍam Rāüḷ) and Cakradhar.
The devatās — the gods of the Vedas and Purāṇas — are powerful beings who can grant only worldly fruit; worshipping them binds, so it is forbidden.
Renunciation (saṃnyāsa) with wandering, begging and strict non-violence is the ideal, open to women and to all castes; caste distinctions and Vedic ritual are rejected.
Devotion is through remembrance of the incarnations' līlās and through places and relics they touched (sthāna, sambandha).
Marathi is the sacred language; the scriptures were long kept secret in special scripts.
summary: The Mahānubhāva panth, founded in 13th-c. Maharashtra by Cakradhar Svāmī, worships one Supreme (Parameśvara) incarnated as the five Kṛṣṇas and rejects the worship of all other gods, caste and Vedic ritual. Its Marathi prose scriptures — the Līḷācaritra and Sūtrapāṭh — are among the oldest Marathi literature; its monks and nuns live by renunciation, wandering and non-violence.

name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma

scholarly.text: late 15th – 16th c.; sattra network from the 16th–17th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as supreme scripture
a non-dual reading of the Bhāgavata through Śrīdhara Svāmin's commentary

distinctive_positions: Single refuge (eka-śaraṇa) in Kṛṣṇa alone: no other deity is worshipped, and Vedic ritual and animal sacrifice are rejected.
The name (nāma) is the chief means; of the nine forms of devotion, hearing (śravaṇa) and singing (kīrtana) are foremost.
The four real things (cāri vastu): the name, God (deva), the guru and the community of devotees (bhakta).
Devotion is that of the servant (dāsya); Rādhā is not worshipped and the erotic mood is not cultivated.
The true devotee does not desire even liberation.
In the nāmghar and sattra a sacred book — the Bhāgavata (or the Kīrtana-ghoṣā) — sits on the guru-āsana in place of an image.
Initiation (śaraṇ) is open to all castes, tribes and to Muslims; the sattras house celibate (kevaliyā) and married devotees.
Drama (bhāonā), song (bargīt) and dance are forms of worship.
summary: The Ekaśaraṇa ('single refuge') Dharma of Assam, founded by Śaṅkaradeva (1449–1568 by tradition) and continued by Mādhavadeva, teaches exclusive servant-devotion to Kṛṣṇa through his name, the guru and the congregation, without images, other gods or Vedic rites. Its scriptures — the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, the Nām-ghoṣā, the bargīts and one-act plays — are sung and performed in village nāmghars and in the sattras (monasteries), which after Mādhavadeva divided into four saṃhatis.

name: Brahma saṃhati (Dāmodarīyā)
distinctive_positions: Traces itself to the brahmins Dāmodaradeva and Harideva; brahmin sattrādhikārs.
More accommodating of image worship and of brahmanical rites than the other saṃhatis.
Bhaṭṭadeva's prose renderings of the Bhāgavata and Gītā belong to it.
summary: The saṃhati of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras descended from Dāmodaradeva and Harideva, with brahmin leadership and greater accommodation of brahmanical practice; it includes several of the great Majuli sattras patronised by the Ahom kings (identification of individual sattras to verify).

name: Puruṣa saṃhati
distinctive_positions: Led by Śaṅkaradeva's grandsons Puruṣottama and Caturbhuja Ṭhākur.
Emphasis on the name and on Śaṅkaradeva's own line.
summary: The saṃhati of the sattras led by Śaṅkaradeva's descendants, above all his grandsons Puruṣottama and Caturbhuja Ṭhākur.

name: Kāla saṃhati
distinctive_positions: Founded by Gopāla Ātā of Bhavānīpur (seat at Kālajhār).
Strongly guru-centred and egalitarian, drawing many low-caste and tribal followers; the Māyāmarā (Moāmoriyā) sattra of Aniruddhadeva belonged to it.
summary: The saṃhati founded by Gopāla Ātā, a disciple of Mādhavadeva, marked by intense devotion to the guru and wide recruitment among low castes and tribes.

name: Nikā saṃhati
distinctive_positions: Emphasis on ritual cleanliness and strict conduct (nikā = clean).
Traced to disciples of Mādhavadeva such as Mathurādāsa Ātā and Badulā Padma Ātā (names to verify).
summary: The saṃhati emphasising purity and discipline of conduct, traced to disciples of Mādhavadeva.

name: Rāmdāsī sampradāya (Samartha sampradāya)
regions: Maharashtra (Sajjangaḍ, Cāphaḷ, Jāmb, Śivthar, the eleven Māruti temples)
distinctive_positions: Worship of Rāma and of Māruti (Hanumān) as the embodiment of strength and service; the thirteen-syllable mantra 'śrī rām jay rām jay jay rām'.
Devotion joined to discriminating knowledge of the self (Advaita in the Dāsbodh) and to vigilant, effortful action in the world (prayatna).
The seeker passes through the conditions of the bound, the seeker, the practitioner and the accomplished.
The ideal leader (mahant) organises, teaches and protects dharma; physical strength is cultivated.
The mind is instructed directly (Manāce Śloka).
summary: The Samartha sampradāya founded by Samartha Rāmdās (1608–1681/82) of Maharashtra: devotion to Rāma and Hanumān, discrimination of the self, disciplined effort and service to society, taught in the Dāsbodh and the Manāce Śloka and organised through maṭhs and Māruti temples.

name: Unaffiliated regional bhakti poets (classificatory grouping)
distinctive_positions: Not a sampradāya: a grouping made by this ontology for vernacular devotional poets who founded no order and are claimed by several traditions.
Common ground: the name, the saints' company, love and longing for a personal God (Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Veṅkaṭeśvara), often joined to a non-dual vision ('you alone appear in all forms').
notes: Created by U26 so that teachers without a sampradāya of their own can be recorded; convergence counts should not treat it as an independent lineage root. See REPORT.md.
summary: A classificatory grouping (not a tradition) for regional devotional poets in U26's scope — Narsinh Mehta (Gujarati), Annamācārya, Tyāgarāja and Bhadrācala Rāmadās (Telugu), Caṇḍīdās (Bengali) and Vidyāpati (Maithili) — each also linked to the traditions that claim them.
